newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd's offer seen unconditional on acceptances.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's offer seen unconditional on acceptances.

text.p: Lloyd's of London is on Friday expected to announce that a 3.2 billion pounds settlement offer to investors is unconditional as to acceptances, the strongest indicator yet that its recovery plan will proceed as planned.

The 300-year old insurance market's ruling council, led by chairman David Rowland, was poised on Thursday afternoon to approve this decision, having received acceptances from over 90 percent of Lloyd's 34,000 investors worldwide, called Names.
Other conditions will need to be met before the entire package can go ahead, including British government approval.
The insurance market is also likely to extend, possibly even for a few weeks, a deadline for Names to accept the settlement offer after declaring it unconditional, said industry sources.
Under its recovery proposals, Lloyd's aims to reinsure billions of pounds in liabilities into a new company Equitas.
The settlement offer, which has been raised to 3.2 billion pounds from 2.8 billion three months ago, is designed to soften the cost to Names of setting up Equitas and to end litigation.
By the original noon on Wednesday voting deadline, the offer had won overwhelming support from British Names, who account for around four fifths of the membership worldwide.

There was around two-thirds acceptance among American Names, hundreds of whom waited until Lloyd's on Tuesday evening managed to overturn a potentially ruinous U.S. court ruling against it before flooding the market's headquarters with faxed "Yes" votes.
Lloyd's not only needed convincing majority support to declare the offer unconditional, but had to secure the backing of two key blocks of Names: the litigants and the major debtors.
The British government is likely to decide next week whether to approve the recovery plan and the solvency of Lloyd's. The success of the settlement offer was crucial to this decision.
If and when it does this, events may move very quickly. Equitas itself could go "live" within two weeks and may be just days away from taking on the claims and liabilities it will handle.
A significant chunk of these are likely to be pollution, asbestosis and health-related claims in the U.S., some of them dating back to policies written late last century.
Lloyd's also has to file solvency statements with the U.S. Treasury and New York Department of Insurance in September.
The formalities might seem an anti-climax after the drama of two eleventh-hour court cases brought against the market trying to stop the plan -- one in Britain and one in the United States.
Images of a battered and weary centuries old insurance market rising from the ashes will also be misplaced, as Lloyd's has already been undergone a dramatic transformation.

Lloyd's problems began in the 1980s when a destructive combination of negligent underwriting, poor investment advice and a sequence of natural disasters conspired to bring about losses of several billion pounds between 1988 and 1992.
Since then, however, the market has swung back into the black, announcing in July a profit of nearly 1.1 billion pounds for the 1993 year of account.
